text: Tradition says that in old age, Chandragupta gave up his throne, became a Jain monk, and
died at Shravana Belagola in Karnataka.
His grandson became the most famous ruler in Indian history, Ashoka.
In about 261 BCE, Ashoka invaded Kalinga in today's Odisha.
He won, and the cost horrified him.
We know this because Ashoka told us himself. In an inscription carved in stone, he says
a hundred thousand people were killed and a hundred fifty thousand were carried away.
Then he wrote something almost no conqueror ever wrote. He was sorry.
taking off his goggles. An emperor, apologizing. In stone. Read that twice.
Ashoka turned to the teachings of the Buddha. He called his new policy, Dhamma.
Kindness, tolerance between religions, care for animals, wells and shade trees along the roads.
He carved his messages on rocks and tall stone pillars across the empire
in a script called Brahmi. For centuries after, nobody could read it. Until 1837, when a British
scholar James Prinsep cracked it, and Ashoka suddenly spoke again. One of his pillars
at Sarnath was topped with four lions standing back to back. You know it, it's on every
Indian banknote and passport, India's national emblem. And the wheel beneath the lions, the
Ashoka Chakra, sits in the middle of India's flag, two thousand years later. Still on the flag!
But empires built by one great man rarely outlive him for long. About 50 years after Ashoka died,
the last Morya emperor was killed by his own channel during a military parade.
